p: We’re going to stage it so that it does have the least disruption, but we’ll get back to you the specifics on that.
Sure. And a follow-up which we can cover then, is will riders be able to continue utilizing the stop while the construction is underway?
Yes, we’re not going to close the stop.
Okay, great. And will there be any impact on ferry ridership or revenue levels?

We’re hoping– during construction, we hope not, because we’re going to try

to stage it accordingly. We don’t want it to impact ridership. Ridership is incredibly important for us, but we’re also hoping that with the completion of the construction that it’ll increase ridership because there’ll be more people that will be able to que [sic] there.

Thank you. And on the cost side, do you have any information you can share on ridership trends? I know ridership is up, I believe. But that as well as the per-passenger subsidy that we expect for this year?

Yes. So, ridership was at an all-time high when as we’ve had a little bit of a hit because of the terrible cold winter that we had. I don’t know if you had– we had to stop service a couple of days because there was ice. But ridership is still very high. It’s a really beloved, very popular way of people going from place to place, and we want to continue to be that way. The Rockaway Rocket has become more and more popular as well. So, we’re really excited about how the ferry has done. The price per subsidy is about– the price for subsidy per passenger is about $8.33, and it’s lower than any other ferry passenger across the country as well as

the Long Island Railroad or Metro North. So, we’re really proud of that. It’s down 30 percent since the start of the ferry. So we’ve worked really hard to make sure that that price per subsidy has gone down, and we’re running the ferries financially efficient.
And do we expect that the shifting cost of fuel to have an impact on that per passenger subsidy, or an increase in cost this coming summer in particular?
Yeah, we do have a fuel hedging strategy. So, some of that we’ve hedged and mitigated, but I will have to get back to you on exactly the impact.
One of the questions I have is I believe in fiscal year 2025 there was an operating deficit of roughly $15 million. Is that correct?
An operating–
[interposing] Or the operating deficit of the ferry.

So, the ferry technically runs at a deficit and it’s subsidized by other revenue, and that is some of our rental revenue that we get for some of the assets that we manage at EDC

directly goes to subsidize that ferry. I don’t know if that’s what you’re referring to. So, there’s not a deficit because we subsidize it.
The deficit prior to tapping into EDC’s cash reserves.

No, the– I’m not sure what you’re referring to, but again, we– this subsidy is there as a stable source of revenue, and again, it’s part of our maritime assets and our 42nd Street assets that subsidize the revenue that we get from those rental properties subsidize the ferry. So, don’t– so the deficit is basically the subsidy, but we don’t have an additional deficit over that.
Okay. And is there an effort to look at increasing New York City ferry revenues to try to help that, decrease that subsidy?

We’re always looking to increase the financial efficiency of NYC ferry. I think the increased ridership– there are other ways of like– wifi sponsorship, etcetera, that other ways for us to increase the ferry revenue. Ultimately, it is going to be all transit is subsidized, and so we are realistic in understanding that it’s such a

beloved form of transit for New Yorkers that it will require subsidy.

Earlier this year, I know there were efforts to acquire a corporate sponsor. Did EDC receive any submissions or proposals for private entities to be a corporate sponsor and sort of help with that revenue subsidy issue?

Yeah. So, we’re always looking for partnerships to help NYC ferry. We did receive some submissions that did not like have a maximum benefit for what they were offering, and so we decided not to go with any of the submissions.
And have you received revenue from ferry sponsors in the past, and if so, how much?
We’ve [inaudible] inside the ferries, etcetera, and it’s about $300,000. In 2025, it was about $300,000.
And is that continuing?
Yes.

My last question is around AI and tech. In January 2025, there was the

Artificial Intelligence Advantage Report that EDC recognized New York City as the applied AI capital of the world with 40,000 AI-ready workers, active investors, over 2,000 AI start-ups. Do you have an updated figure on how we’re performing in terms of AI readiness?
We will have to get back to you on that. I don’t have that right now.

And as a follow-up, would love to hear what steps EDC took to accomplish some of the priorities that were outlined in that report around fostering new business creation and partnership to build this AI ecosystem, developing a diverse AI-ready workforce to power the future economy and apply– or position New York as a global leader for applied AI. So, would love to follow up with the key steps that EDC has taken to achieve the priorities outlined in your report, any programming to train workforces on the development of AI-ready skills and any city funds being deployed to bolster the AI workforce or help develop AI-related businesses.
We’ll get back to you on that. Thank you.
Thank you. Back to the Chair.
Thank you. And a hearing would not be complete without Council Member Restler. So, I’m going to toss it to him, and then I just have a couple last questions after, but– no, no, no, go, go, go.

Okay. Thank you, Chair Lee, for making me laugh and for doing such a great job leading these hearings. It’s great to join you and Chair Maloney. Thank you to the EDC team for being here as well. I’ll say one nice thing first which is not what I– I don’t do that at every hearing. I am very grateful to Jennifer Sun [sp?] and some of her colleagues for joining us in Dumbo recently to try to help us better manage tourism in the neighborhood and EDC’s willingness to kind of be a creative partner and go outside of what might be its traditional roles to try and help address needs and issues in our community is appreciated. Some other city agencies that were asked to help declined. So, we appreciate EDC for stepping up and working with us, and I really want to thank you for that.
We love Jennifer Sun as well.

She’s great and she’s really done– I’ve been really appreciative. Other thing I will say just to put a marker down, I am deeply concerned about jobs in New York City, and as I look across my district on the kind of waterfront in Brooklyn, downtown Brooklyn, the office market is just incredibly weak, and we need to be developing new economic development strategies to revitalize downtown Brooklyn and Dumbo, where we have buildings that are 80 percent vacant right now. So, we’re working on a white paper ourselves with some expert help, but really want to make this a priority partnership opportunity with EDC in the months to come where we try to ensure that our communities are really dynamic 24/7, live/work communities. They’re just filling up the live part right now. Onto my topic of choice, maybe my favorite issue to raise with my friends at EDC is Stop the Chop. I know you’re surprised. You know, we have a socialist mayor who has committed his support for Stopping the Chop and we’d love to start to see the elimination of non-essential helicopter travel from the city’s

helipads. Last year, the Ryder Cup was in New Jersey, I think, and we had helicopters going– or no, it must have been Long Island. The Ryder Cup was in Long Island, excuse me. I don’t follow golf. But I did experience it because there were helicopters leaving every five minutes from the city’s helipads going over– very low over our community and making it impossible for people to have a conversation outside on the street, on their stoop and their backyard. Are we expecting similar amounts of extremely disruptive helicopter travel for the World Cup?

So, the World Cup is eight games here. We have– EDC runs two heliports in Midtown and then downtown Skyport. The Midtown has special permits so it can be only open for certain hours. The Downtown we worked very closely with the community members to reduce those hours, and so– it’s a public–

[interposing] I’m aware of the changes that have been made and they have really not helped in my community where we continue to get an enormous amount of incoming where people struggle in Brooklyn Ridge Park, they struggle

just to be in their own property because of the extreme noise that’s created by helicopters. So, I–
[interposing] Yeah. It’s a public– it’s a public– the Downtown Skyport is a public heliport, so we cannot not allow people to land.

Not allow people to land. You could regulate the type of travel that’s happening from the heliport. You don’t need to allow folks to go to the Hamptons or JFK on helicopter rides. You don’t need to allow tourism trips from there. I certainly have no problem with people taking a helicopter if they need to– for health reasons or if there’s some sort of public benefit like news helicopters or NYPD helicopters. But the idea that we pollute our environment, it’s the equivalent of 40 cars idling on the street, one helicopter above ground, and then create such extreme noise that people can’t have conversations. You know, so the– the top one-tenth of one percent can get to the Hampton’s faster or get to JFK faster, I find that deeply offensive. So, I strongly support the banning of all non-essential travel from the heliports that you all control, and I’m trying to

understand can we do anything to limit the helicopter activity out for the World Cup, and are there other ways that EDC is looking at limiting these types of really egregious and disruptive helicopter activity from your helipads?

Yeah. This is under FAA purview, but I would say that just looking at– we hear your concerns. And just looking ahead, we are looking to EV tolls, and so we have– hopefully the pilot will get by the end of this year, and the FAA will approve like EV tolls. And I don’t know if you came to our demonstration, but they’re very, very quiet. I mean, all electric–

[interposing] Yeah. I mean, I haven’t flown in one, but I saw them on the east side not too long ago with some of my friends– you know, Botcher and Powers and others were out there. What, should I not– were you out there, too? No? No. She couldn’t make it. Chair missed it, but she– but I’m glad to hear that they’re quieter and they’re better for the environment. If that all works, God bless. I don’t have any objection. But what I do have an objection to is the status quo and our insistence on maintaining it and allowing for

these incredibly disruptive helicopters to pollute and disrupt our communities all day, every day, I think is really bad policy, and I think we’re favoring the extreme elite at the expense of everybody else, and I think we should stop it. I think we should discontinue this helicopter activity immediately, and once the EV tolls are ready, bring them in and let the rich people travel around that way.
Understood
Thank you.

Thank you. Really quickly, a couple of follow-ups. Earlier you mentioned the grocery store site submission form is open for applications. So, how are you planning on incentivizing the private owners to possibly use their sites, or their– you know, if they have properties or if they have land, how would you incentivize them to apply?

Yeah. So we are getting the word out there, so please, you know, help us get the word out there. We are doing a big marketing campaign. So, we’ve had quite a lot of– you can see how many people have gone on and looked at it. So,

it just opened, so we’re still gathering information, but that’s how we’re getting the word, just by marketing and also direct emails, because we know a lot of these property owners and brokers to ensure that the word is getting out there.

Perfect. And just my last question, because I’d be remiss coming from the nonprofit sector without bringing up the capital projects that run through EDCfrom the nonprofit perspective. Because I think we got awarded city funds in– I say we because I still feel like I’m part of the nonprofit community, but got awarded funding in 2018, and they literally I think just got their CP like a month ago, right? And so when I think about the fact that these organizations need the space and the renovation and the funding to provide services to the community, not for a for-profit benefit or reason, plus you know, I think with cost– like, if we’re talking about savings and just cost, the fact that all that time has passed, you know. The cost has gone up. The funding hasn’t, right? And so what ends up happening is the scope of work has to continually decrease, and it just, you know, is a drain on the nonprofit organizations where they have

to take out high interest loans. So, the total cost of the projects end up costing the city more, and so I’m just wondering from your perspective if there– I get that there’s regulations and that there’s processes that need to happen and checks and balances with OMB, but back then when I was still at my organization I have to say EDC was great in the sense that they– the staffers we were working with at EDC felt really bad for us, because a lot of it was not on us. Like, we were submitting all the paperwork, it’s just that the process itself is so cumbersome a lot of times. And so I’m just wondering from your perspective if there are ways that we can look at perhaps– not foregoing regulation but also streamlining some of it so that it doesn’t take as long for these groups to get their funding. So, I just wanted to get your thoughts on that.

Yeah, that’s through our funding agreements which is a fantastic group, and they work really closely as you said with the nonprofits and applicants, and I think, you know, people really– nonprofits want to go through EDC because we take that very tailored approach and we try to move things on very quickly. There’s very

strict rules with these grants. It’s on a reimbursement basis. There’s so much paperwork as you can imagine, and has to go through OMB and OMB Counsel. So there is a lot of process, but yes, you know, we recognize that it can be a hardship for nonprofits. I mean, EDC has a lot of capital projects that we do on behalf of our assets as well as DOT parks and libraries, and so we’re not in a dissimilar situation, and so we really work hard to building a very close relationship with OMB so we can move these CPs as much as we– as fast as we possibly can, but as you can imagine, it is a process with limited staff on their side. So, but we will continue to look at that and try to make sure that– we understand the burden it has on nonprofits.

Yeah, and if there’s any sort of taskforce or group internally that can look at this periodically, I think that’d be great because it’s just– I just– I cannot tell you how badly I feel because these organizations are just trying to do good work on the ground and then they get stuck with all this paperwork and then can’t do things. So, I ended up having to be a professional fundraiser or event planner because I had so many,

you know– like I had– it’s like, okay, we just did a capital campaign and then we’re doing another one, and the community is like, didn’t we just submit– you know, didn’t we just give you guys donations for capital campaign? I’m like, yeah, but you know, there’s all these extra costs. And so would love to have that feedback if you could.
Yeah, we’d be happy to work on that.

Okay, perfect. And I think– does anyone have any other questions? Yeah. [inaudible] Well, if you think of more we can always submit after and then ask for follow-up. So, and I think with that we are done with– what are we on, day four of hearings? So, I can gavel out, but thank you so much.
Thank you.

Dear Chair Louis and Subcommittee Members,

On behalf of the Association for a Better New York (ABNY), a non-profit dedicated to the advancement and support of New York City, I am writing to express our support for the proposed rezoning of the Dewitt Clinton Park North sites at 801 11th Avenue and 629 West 54th Street. The project represents a critical step forward in addressing New York City’s ongoing housing crisis while delivering meaningful benefits to the local community.

The Chapman Group and Friedland Properties’ proposed development will yield just over 1,000 new housing units, a full 25% of which will be designated as much-needed affordable units. At a time when the demand for housing far exceeds supply, projects like this are not just beneficial but essential. The additional residential use will also positively contribute to increasing the vitality and 24-7 nature to this corner of Manhattan.

Importantly, the project has been thoughtfully designed to minimize potential impacts on the surrounding neighborhood. For example, it will not cast shadows on Dewitt Clinton Park, preserving this much-loved public space for the community’s enjoyment. Additionally, the new project is proposed without displacing the existing auto showrooms in the commercial space ensures the retention of high-paying local jobs and supports the area’s economic activity.

Additionally, significant financial investment via the air rights purchase from the Hudson River Park Trust will directly support critical projects that enhance the park, ensuring it continues to thrive as a vital resource for all New Yorkers. This collaboration between private development and public infrastructure improvement is a model of responsible and community-centered urban planning. The Trust has been an incredible steward of this world-class park for decades and we are thrilled to see this project support its efforts, contributing to improvements in the park that visitors from across the entire city will benefit from.

We urge the Council to support the requested actions and thank you for considering our support.

Sincerely,

Chad Purkey Vice President

Testimony of Noreen Doyle President & CEO, Hudson River Park Trust Regarding DeWitt Clinton Park North Land Use Applications (801 Eleventh Avenue and 629 West 54th Street) May 27, 2026

Good morning. My name is Noreen Doyle and I am the President and CEO of the Hudson River Park Trust. I am speaking today regarding both DeWitt Clinton Park North projects – 801 Eleventh Avenue and 629 West 54th Street. Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

As you may know, the Trust is a legislatively created partnership between New York State and New York City created for the purpose of designing and building Hudson River Park along four miles of the Manhattan shoreline and operating the park on a financially self-supporting basis to the extent practicable. The Special Hudson River Park District is a valuable tool that has to date generated approximately $151 million for park infrastructure from three previous development rights transfers. The Trust has used these funds to perform essential structural repairs at Pier 40, to construct new public restrooms in Chelsea, to help build a new public park pier at Pier 97 in Hell’s Kitchen, and to advance park improvements that are currently in design between West 29th and 44th Streets.

In consultation with Manhattan Community Board 4 (CB4), the Trust has identified Pier 76 as the priority use for the contemplated development rights proceeds under from the two transfers contemplated in the projects under consideration. Pier 76 is located opposite the Javits Convention Center in an area that has very little public open space. Until 2021, when it became part of Hudson River Park, Pier 76 was used by NYPD as Manhattan’s tow pound. Today, it is essentially a large swath of asphalt, measures more than 5.5 acres, and is supported by 6,500 wooden piles that are deteriorating as I speak. It needs to be completely rebuilt which, given its scale, will be very costly. The Trust has secured a commitment of $85 million from NYS towards this goal, and we are working towards an eventual match from NYC as well as funding provided by the Trust, including the proceeds from the sale of development rights that may be authorized under these projects.

Unlike previous transfers, the Trust is not able to advance its own legislatively required public significant action process concurrently with ULURP

as the developers do not yet have a committed closing or construction schedule for their projects. For this reason, and with the encouragement of CB4 and the cooperation of the developers, the Trust has built certain protections into its agreements, including establishing minimum prices for eventual purchases and securing a commitment from the developers that they will not look elsewhere to purchase the development rights. In response to questions from CB4 related to their review of the two ULURP applications, the Trust wrote to CB4 Chair Leslie Boghosian Murphy on January 30, 2026 letter, in part as follows:

“Given uncertainty around timing, the Trust has negotiated a separate protective agreement with the developers, supplementing the Department of City Planning restrictive declaration that will condition access to approved FAR and use rights on payment to the Trust. Under this agreement, if during the term of the special permit (including potential extensions) the City approves zoning changes affecting the receiving sites, or if transferable development rights from other sources become available that would allow additional development beyond what was permitted as-of-right prior to ULURP approval, the developers would nonetheless remain obligated to proceed under the ULURP special permit and to purchase the authorized quantity of development rights from the Trust. This provision ensures that payment supporting critical park improvements cannot be avoided if the developers elect to proceed during this ten-year period.”

For your further information, and the record, I have attached copies of the referenced protective agreements, one between the Trust and 760 12th LLC (for the development at 629 West 54th Street) and the other between the Trust and 801 11th Ave., LLC (for the development at 801 11th Avenue).

Should the developers elect to proceed following assumed ULURP approvals, the Trust must conduct its own mandatory public review process and complete appraisals to determine values of the development rights. At that time, in the quite unlikely event that the development rights proceeds are no longer needed for Pier 76 given the scale of needs I have described, the Trust has committed to engage in a future discussion with CB4 and others about their desires for the use of the transfer proceeds within the CB4 section of the Park, focusing first on the Hell’s Kitchen area as has been requested.

Again, thank you for this opportunity to share how the proposed projects could benefit public open space for all New Yorkers and visitors.

Public Comments of Save The Inlet Opposing the Upzoning Proposed for 40-56 Quay Street Save the Inlet is a part of the Friends of Bushwick Inlet Park, an all-volunteer, parks and environmental advocacy group based in Greenpoint and Williamsburg. Our mission is to develop the Bushwick Inlet Park into a resilient, world-class public park on the North Brooklyn waterfront. We are committed to environmentally sound park design and believe that parks are the great equalizer. Through our programming and work we strive to sustain the open space that is Bushwick Inlet Park and to create a welcoming environment for everyone. Our commitment to create this park is a sustained one. In 2002, as part of 197-A planning, the community conceived of an expansive waterfront park that encompassed the Quay Street parcels. In 2005, the community secured a promise from New York City to build a smaller park along the waterfront adjacent to the Bushwick Inlet as part of a larger rezoning. After twelve additional years of community efforts, in 2017, the City purchased the final parcel of land needed to fulfill that promise. Yet, nearly a decade later, the park remains largely unbuilt while the waterfront around it has filled with luxury towers. We submit this statement to urge the Borough President to vote against the Monitor Point proposal on Quay Street. While land use decisions often involve careful balancing of competing public policy goals, it is stunningly poor public planning to approve a massive upzoning on government agency land to build still more largely luxury housing within the floodplain along our community’s waterfront. This is especially true given Monitor Point’s many requests for exceptions from environmental protections, and placement adjacent both to the fragile Bushwick Inlet and the community’s dream park. What’s more, despite its use of government land, the Monitor Point proposal brazenly promises just the bare minimum of affordable units allowable under law, provides an impermeable podium for a luxury tower and mixed rate tower, and leaves a segregated affordable tower (which would depend on unsecured HPD funding) more exposed. The proposed project is inequitable, short-sighted, and irreversible. Save the Inlet also seeks the Borough President’s support for the MTA parcel to be used as parkland to provide climate resiliency and protection for the people, ecology and existing infrastructure within our community and to buffer the Bushwick Inlet. This use is consistent with planning priorities endorsed by the government at every level, and

the climate change realities we all see.
